model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to describe a festival in my town. It is a river festival and it happens every year in September, at the end of the summer.

So last year I took part in it. Normally I just go and watch, but last year my aunt has a food stall, so I helped her. We started very early in the morning, and we made pancakes, I think maybe two hundred, it was a lot. The stall was next to the river, so we can see everything.

In the evening people put lanterns on the water. There is music, and everybody walks along the river together. I also meet my old school friend there, we didn't see each other for a long time, so that was nice.

I enjoyed it very much because it was different. When you work in the festival you see many things that other people don't see. Also I was very tired but happy. The town is usually quiet, but on this day it is not quiet, everybody is outside. So it was a very good day and this is the festival I took part in.

'Nice', 'good', 'a lot', 'different' — the whole evaluation runs on flat words.
Almost every link is 'so' or 'also', and the close restates the card.

annotations.label: Two tenses missing at once

model_answers.label: The target — same day, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about the river festival in my home town, which happens every year at the end of the summer — and specifically about last September, because that was the first year I actually took part in it rather than just turning up to watch.

My aunt runs a food stall there, and she'd asked me back in August whether I'd give her a hand, so I said yes without really thinking about what that would involve. What it involved was a six o'clock start. She'd already been up mixing batter by the time I arrived, and by lunchtime we'd turned out something like two hundred pancakes between us. I'd more or less stopped being able to feel my arms.

The stall was right on the riverbank, though, which meant we had easily the best view in town. At dusk everybody brings paper lanterns down to the water and floats them out, and there's a procession along both banks with a brass band at the front. By about eight the whole thing was in full swing. I also bumped into a friend I hadn't seen since school, which I wasn't expecting at all.

What I enjoyed most, though, wasn't the lanterns — it was being on the inside of it. When you're behind a stall you notice things you'd never notice as a visitor: who knows everybody, which families have been doing the same thing for years, and how much work sits underneath three hours that are supposed to look effortless. I'd watched that festival my whole life, and I'd never once thought about who was putting it on.

'Give her a hand', 'in full swing', 'bumped into' replace 'nice' and 'good'.
A cleft announces the fourth bullet, so the evaluation cannot be skipped.

annotations.label: Past perfect plus reported question

annotations.label: Two layers of past time
annotations.why: Use one 'by the time' sentence per story to show sequencing.

annotations.why: Reuse it for any event at its busiest — a market, a party, a match.

annotations.label: Phrasal verb doing precise work
annotations.why: 'Bumped into' says by chance in two words; 'met accidentally' does not.

annotations.label: Cleft opens the last bullet
annotations.why: Naming the move out loud stops you skipping the 'explain' line entirely.

annotations.label: A list of three

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The one I want to talk about is a river festival my home town has been putting on for as long as anyone can remember, always at the tail end of the summer. Last September was the first year I was on the working side of it rather than the wandering-around side.

My aunt has had a food stall there for the best part of a decade, and she'd asked me in August whether I'd help out, which I'd agreed to before I'd properly thought it through. Thinking it through would have meant noticing the six o'clock start. She was already mixing batter by the time I turned up, and by the middle of the day we'd produced somewhere in the region of two hundred pancakes and I had no feeling left in my forearms.

What the stall did give us was the riverbank, which is where the whole thing actually happens. At dusk people float paper lanterns out onto the water and a procession works its way along both banks behind a fairly ragged brass band.

Not that the lanterns were the part that stayed with me. What stayed with me was the view from behind the stall, because from there you see the machinery. You see which families have been running the same three metres of pavement for thirty years, and how much unglamorous work sits underneath something that is meant to look spontaneous. I'd watched that festival every year of my life without once wondering who was making it happen.

what_lifts_it.point: Present perfect continuous and a stacked past perfect where band 7 used one layer.
'The tail end', 'in the region of', 'the machinery' — idiom placed, not displayed.
The close names what the story is an example of instead of summarising it.

annotations.label: Perfect continuous for duration
annotations.why: Use it once for anything still going on now that started long ago.

annotations.span: which I'd agreed to before I'd properly thought it through
annotations.label: Two past perfects in one clause
annotations.why: Stack them only where the order genuinely matters, as it does here.

annotations.span: at the tail end of the summer
annotations.label: Idiom sitting naturally
annotations.why: Two well-placed idioms beat five decorative ones every single time.

annotations.span: from there you see the machinery
annotations.label: One metaphor carries the point
annotations.why: 'The machinery' says hidden organised effort without a single extra clause.

annotations.span: I'd watched that festival every year of my life without once wondering who was making it happen.
annotations.label: Close lifts out of the anecdote
annotations.why: End on what the story is an example of, not on what happened.

model_answers.label: A typical band 6 answer
model_answers.transcript:
I would like to describe a song which reminds me of one place. It is an old song with guitar. I don't know the name of the band exactly, but my brother is playing it all the time.

The place is a campsite near the sea. When I was nineteen I work there for the summer, in the kitchen. My brother has a van and he drives me there every morning, and this song is always on. So now when I hear it I remember this road and I remember the sea.

The summer was very hard because we work many hours and the money was not good. But it was also very nice, because we were young and we have no responsibility.

Two years ago I heard this song in a supermarket. It was very strange, because for one moment I am not in the supermarket, I am in the van again. I think music can do this and other things cannot do this. So this is the song, and this is the reason it is special for me.

what_caps_it.point: The past narrative slides into the present in five separate places.
'Very hard', 'not good', 'very nice', 'very strange' — adjectives with 'very' in front.
Two sentences repeat almost word for word, and the close restates the card.

annotations.span: for one moment I am not in the supermarket, I am in the van again
annotations.label: Shows the effect, doesn't state it
annotations.why: Keep this — showing the moment is worth more than saying 'it was emotional'.

annotations.span: my brother is playing it all the time
annotations.label: Present continuous for a past habit
annotations.why: Use 'he'd play it constantly' — 'would' is the natural form for repeated past.

annotations.span: I work there for the summer
annotations.label: Bare present inside a past clause
annotations.why: 'When I was nineteen I worked there' — both halves must agree.

annotations.span: we have no responsibility
annotations.label: Tense slips again at the end
annotations.why: 'We had nothing to worry about' keeps the tense and improves the phrase.

annotations.span: So this is the song, and this is the reason it is special for me.
annotations.label: Ending recycles the prompt
annotations.why: Finish on an idea about music, not on a restatement of the task.

model_answers.label: Same summer, band 7 language
model_answers.transcript:
The piece of music I'd pick is a fairly slow guitar track that my older brother used to play constantly. I couldn't tell you the name of the band even now, which probably says something about how I came across it in the first place.

It's tied to one specific place: a campsite on the coast about two hours from where we grew up. The summer I turned nineteen I worked there in the kitchen, and my brother had a van and a job on the same site, so he'd drive us both over at seven every morning with that album on. By the end of August I must have heard it a couple of hundred times, and I'd honestly stopped noticing it at all.

It was a hard summer — long shifts, terrible pay, and the two of us sharing a tent that leaked whenever it rained. But it's also the last summer I can remember having absolutely nothing to worry about, and the song seems to have absorbed all of that. I wouldn't have chosen it as a soundtrack for any of it, but you don't really get to choose.

What gets me is what happened a couple of years ago. I was standing in a supermarket and it came on over the speakers, and for about three seconds I wasn't in the supermarket at all — I was in the passenger seat with the window down. A photograph shows you the place, whereas a song puts you back inside it, and I've never really worked out how that happens.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Would' for repeated past and a modal perfect replace the flat present-tense run.
'Tied to', 'absorbed', 'came on over the speakers' — verbs doing precise work.
A cleft and a 'whereas' contrast give the last forty seconds visible shape.

annotations.span: It's tied to one specific place
annotations.label: Narrows before describing
annotations.why: Announce the link early so the examiner knows where the answer is going.

annotations.span: he'd drive us both over at seven every morning
annotations.label: 'Would' for a repeated past action
annotations.why: Any routine in a past story can take 'd rather than a plain past.

annotations.span: I must have heard it a couple of hundred times
annotations.label: Modal perfect for an estimate
annotations.why: 'Must have' turns a guess into a structure worth grammar credit.

annotations.span: long shifts, terrible pay, and the two of us sharing a tent that leaked
annotations.label: Three details, no verbs wasted
annotations.why: A quick list of three buys ten seconds and sounds deliberate.

annotations.span: the song seems to have absorbed all of that
annotations.label: One verb replaces a sentence
annotations.why: 'Absorbed' does the work of 'it makes me remember all these feelings'.

annotations.span: What gets me is what happened a couple of years ago.
annotations.label: Cleft opens the last bullet
annotations.why: Saying 'what gets me is' commits you to explaining, not describing.

annotations.span: I was in the passenger seat with the window down
annotations.label: Slow down on the image
annotations.why: Drop the pace on the picture so the listener sees it too.

annotations.span: A photograph shows you the place, whereas a song puts you back inside it
annotations.label: Contrast built from two verbs
annotations.why: 'Shows' against 'puts you inside' is sharper than any adjective pair.

model_answers.label: One step further up
model_answers.transcript:
The track I'd go for is a slow, fairly unremarkable guitar piece that my older brother wore out one particular summer. I still couldn't name the band, which tells you that I didn't so much choose this music as get handed it.

What it's welded to is a campsite on the coast, two hours or so from where we grew up. The summer I turned nineteen I was working in the kitchen there, my brother had a van and a job on the same site, and he'd drive us over at seven with that album going. Not once, in three months, did he put anything else on. By September I'd stopped hearing it altogether.

It wasn't a good summer by any sensible measure — the shifts were brutal, the pay was worse, and our tent leaked whenever it rained hard enough to matter. It was, though, the last stretch of my life with nothing hanging over it, and somehow the record has taken all of that on board.

The strange part came years later. I'd have said, if anyone had asked, that I felt nothing whatsoever about that album. Then it started up over the speakers in a supermarket, and for three or four seconds the supermarket simply wasn't there. A photograph hands you a place from the outside; a song drops you back into the middle of it, which is why I think music does something to memory that nothing else quite manages.

what_lifts_it.point: Negative inversion after 'not once' where band 7 used ordinary word order.
'Wore out', 'welded to', 'taken all of that on board' — idiom placed, not paraded.
The close states a general claim about memory rather than the speaker's feeling.

annotations.span: Not once, in three months, did he put anything else on.
annotations.label: Negative inversion
annotations.why: Front a negative adverbial and invert — a single sentence lifts the register.

annotations.span: I didn't so much choose this music as get handed it
annotations.label: 'Not so much... as' structure
annotations.why: Use it whenever you want to correct one description with a better one.

annotations.span: What it's welded to is a campsite on the coast
annotations.label: A stronger verb than 'connected'
annotations.why: 'Welded' says permanent and involuntary in one word.

annotations.span: the record has taken all of that on board
annotations.label: Everyday idiom, exact fit
annotations.why: Common phrasing used precisely outscores rare words used loosely.

annotations.span: which is why I think music does something to memory that nothing else quite manages
annotations.label: Generalises on the way out
annotations.why: Close on the claim your story supports, then stop talking.

model_answers.transcript:
The book I'd recommend is a short novel — barely two hundred pages — that a colleague pushed on me a couple of years ago, more or less insisting I take it home that evening.

It follows a man who leaves his village at eighteen and comes back thirty years later expecting to be recognised. He isn't. His sister is still living there, and she's furious with him in a way he hasn't prepared for at all. That's really the whole plot; there isn't a great deal of incident in it. What there is instead is a lot of quiet, very exact conversation, and a village that has carried on perfectly well without him.

I read the whole thing in a day, on a train, going up to see my parents — five hours each way and nothing else to do. That almost never happens to me. There was no signal on the train, which probably helped more than the book did. I'm normally a slow reader who gives up around page forty.

The reason I'd press it on anyone my age is partly that it's short, which sounds like a weak recommendation until you consider how many people say flatly that they haven't got time to read. The real reason, though, is that it refuses to explain itself. The author sets a scene, gives you two people talking, and leaves. You end up doing about half the work yourself, and I remembered it far better than books that had spelled everything out for me.

model_answers.transcript:
The one I'd hand to someone my age is a short novel, two hundred pages at most, that a colleague more or less forced on me a couple of years back. She wouldn't take no for an answer, which turned out to be sound judgement on her part.

It follows a man who walks out of his village at eighteen and returns three decades later half expecting a welcome. What he gets is indifference. His sister is still in the same house and is angrier than he has any framework for understanding. Very little else happens. What the book consists of is conversation — quiet, exact, and full of things nobody is prepared to say directly.

I read it in a single day on a train, which I can't remember doing before or since. Left to myself I stall somewhere around page forty and never go back. There was no signal on that train either, which I suspect did as much work as the writing.

Why recommend it to people our age in particular. Partly the length, which sounds like faint praise until you count how many of us claim to have no time. Mainly, though, because it declines to explain itself. Scenes are set, people speak, the author withdraws, and the reader is left holding roughly half the meaning. What stayed with me was not the story so much as the discovery that being trusted to work something out is far more memorable than being told it.

model_answers.transcript:
The dish I'd talk about is a lentil and tomato stew — nothing sophisticated, one pan, about forty minutes from start to finish.

I got it from my flatmate's mother, of all people. She lives abroad, and he used to ring her every Sunday, and one week I asked whether she'd talk me through it. So she did, over a video call, while I stood in the kitchen with a notebook. She kept saying that the amounts didn't really matter, which I found quite hard to accept at the time.

I make it about once a week now, usually on a Sunday, so that there's something in the fridge on Monday. You soften an onion, in goes the tomato, then the lentils and a lot of water, and after that you more or less leave it alone. The only thing that matters is not rushing the onion, and that took me roughly six attempts to learn. Everything else about it is forgiving, which is the only reason I still make it.

As for why that particular dish — my first winter here I was living on toast and whatever had been reduced, and I felt fairly grim about the whole thing. My flatmate made this one evening and handed me a bowl, and it was the first thing I'd eaten in that flat that tasted like somebody had bothered. So learning it wasn't really about the recipe. It was about not wanting to go back to living the way I had been.

model_answers.label: Band 8: sustained, not flashy
model_answers.transcript:
The dish is a lentil and tomato stew, which is about as unsophisticated as cooking gets — one pan, four ingredients, three quarters of an hour — and I make more of it than of anything else I know how to make.

It reached me second-hand, from my flatmate's mother, who lives on the other side of the world and whom I have still never met. He rang her every Sunday without fail, and one week I asked whether she'd take me through it. She did, over a video call, while I stood in the kitchen writing down things she plainly thought did not need writing down. Her only real instruction was that the quantities were beside the point, which struck me then as unhelpful and strikes me now as the entire lesson.

These days it's a Sunday job, so that Monday looks after itself. You soften the onion properly — that is the whole trick, and it took me half a dozen goes to stop hurrying it — and everything afterwards is a matter of waiting for it to thicken.

Why this one, though. My first winter here I was living on toast and whatever the supermarket had marked down, and I was fairly miserable without ever quite admitting it. He handed me a bowl of this one evening, and it was the first food in that flat that tasted as though somebody had made an effort. What I actually learned that day had very little to do with lentils.

model_answers.transcript:
I would like to talk about a small café where I take my friends when they come to visit. It is under the railway bridge, near the station, in the old part of the city.

There is not a sign outside. There are six tables and there is a board with the food of the day. Two brothers are working there, they cook and also they serve. Every day there is only one dish, so you cannot choose. Sometimes it is fish, sometimes it is a soup with beans.

model_answers.transcript:
The place I'd take somebody is a café tucked in underneath a railway bridge about five minutes from the main station — the sort of place you'd walk past twice before you found it.

There's no sign, just a doorway and a blackboard propped against the wall. Inside there are six tables, and it's run by two brothers who cook, serve and take the money between them. The blackboard is the whole menu: one dish a day, no choice at all. Some days that's fish, some days it's a bean soup that I'd happily eat every week for the rest of my life. You pay at the counter on the way out, and nobody has ever given me a bill.

I took my cousin there last spring, when she came up for a few days. She'd asked to see something typical, and I could tell from her face on the way in that she thought I'd misunderstood the request. She'd changed her mind by the time the plates arrived. She asked me to write the name down before she left.

The reason I'd choose it over somewhere better known is that the famous places in this city have quietly stopped being for the people who live here. They've been priced for visitors, and the food has been softened to match. In that café, though, you sit next to whoever happens to work on that street, and you eat what they eat. If somebody's only got two days, I'd rather they saw that than a photograph of it.

model_answers.transcript:
If somebody came to stay, I'd take them to a café wedged under a railway arch about five minutes' walk from the station — one of those places you could pass a dozen times without ever registering it.

There is no sign. There's a doorway, a blackboard leaning against the brickwork, and inside, six tables and two brothers who between them do the cooking, the serving and the till. The blackboard is the menu in its entirety: one dish, that day, take it or leave it. Occasionally fish; more often a bean soup I would cheerfully eat until I died. You settle up at the counter on the way out and no bill has ever appeared.

My cousin came up last spring and asked to see something typical, and I could tell as we went in that she suspected me of having misheard her. By the time the plates were down she had revised that view considerably, and she wrote the name down before she left.

What makes me choose it over the well-known places is that those have quietly stopped belonging to the people who live here. Prices have been set with visitors in mind and the cooking has been smoothed out to match, which is a shame but is hardly a mystery. In that café you eat beside whoever works on the street outside, and you eat what they eat. Given two days in a city, I'd sooner show someone that than a tidier version of it.

model_answers.label: Understandable, marks leaking
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about swimming, because I want to be better in swimming.

Now I am not very good. I can swim, but only maybe two hundred metres, and after that I must stop because I am very tired. My technique is not good. I learn to swim when I was a child in a lake, so nobody teach me the correct way.

For improving I think I need lessons. There is a coach in my pool and he gives lessons two times in a week. Also I must practise the breathing, because now I breathe only in one side and this is a problem for my speed.

Why it is important for me? Before, I am running every morning. Then two years ago I hurt my knee and the doctor said no more running. So now swimming is the only sport for me. When I swim my head becomes empty and I feel calm. If I can swim one kilometre without stopping I will be very happy. So this is the sport I want to be better in.

what_caps_it.point: 'Better in swimming', 'breathe in one side' — the wrong preposition, three times over.
A past story told in the present, and third-person -s missing twice.
'Why it is important for me?' is a question standing in for a topic sentence.

annotations.label: Names the real reason plainly
annotations.why: Keep this — the honest personal reason is what makes bullet four work.

annotations.span: I want to be better in swimming
annotations.label: Wrong preposition on the key phrase
annotations.why: 'Better at swimming' — learn 'good at' and 'better at' as fixed pairs.

annotations.span: I learn to swim when I was a child in a lake, so nobody teach me the correct way
annotations.label: Past tense and third-person -s gone
annotations.why: 'I learned... nobody taught me' — both verbs belong in the past.

annotations.span: he gives lessons two times in a week
annotations.label: Frequency phrase built wrongly
annotations.why: 'Twice a week' — 'a week' is the standard form, never 'in a week'.

model_answers.label: Band 7: the same plan, argued
model_answers.transcript:
The activity I'd like to be better at is swimming, which is slightly embarrassing to have to admit at thirty-one.

I can swim, in the sense that I don't sink. What I can't do is swim well. Two hundred metres and I'm hanging off the end of the lane getting my breath back, mainly because my technique has never been corrected. I learned in a lake as a child, by watching my brother and copying him badly, and nobody has told me what I'm doing wrong since. I don't think it has occurred to anybody that it might need saying.

What I'd need to do is fairly obvious, which is the annoying part. There's a coach at my local pool who does technique sessions twice a week, and I'd have to actually go to those rather than telling myself I'll sort it out on my own. The other thing is breathing — I only breathe on one side, which means I swim slightly crooked, and I've been doing it that way for twenty years. Undoing that will be worse than learning it was.

As for why it matters, I used to run every morning, and then I did something fairly permanent to my knee a couple of years ago and had to stop. Swimming's the only thing left that empties my head in the same way. If I could get to a kilometre without stopping, I think I'd have got that back, and I've missed it a great deal more than I expected to.

what_lifts_it.point: A passive present perfect, a perfect continuous and a second conditional in one turn.
'Hanging off the end of the lane', 'empties my head' — concrete instead of abstract.
Each bullet is opened with a phrase that says which bullet is being answered.

annotations.span: I can swim, in the sense that I don't sink. What I can't do is swim well.
annotations.label: Grades the claim precisely
annotations.why: Qualify a claim and then correct it — that is what an honest self-assessment sounds like.

annotations.span: my technique has never been corrected
annotations.label: Passive present perfect
annotations.why: The passive puts the blame nowhere, which is exactly the meaning wanted.

annotations.span: hanging off the end of the lane getting my breath back
annotations.label: A picture, not an adjective
annotations.why: Describe what exhaustion looks like rather than saying you were tired.

annotations.span: What I'd need to do is fairly obvious, which is the annoying part.
annotations.label: Signposts and evaluates at once
annotations.why: Announcing the bullet and judging it buys you both structure and opinion.

annotations.span: I've been doing it that way for twenty years
annotations.label: Perfect continuous shows the span
annotations.why: Reach for it whenever a habit began long ago and is running still.

annotations.span: As for why it matters
annotations.label: Opens the last bullet
annotations.why: Three words that guarantee you answer the 'explain' line.

annotations.span: I did something fairly permanent to my knee
annotations.label: Understatement doing real work
annotations.why: Playing an injury down sounds far more natural than dramatising it.

annotations.span: I've missed it a great deal more than I expected to
annotations.label: Falls away on the last clause
annotations.why: Let the pitch drop through 'than I expected to' so the turn closes.

model_answers.label: Band 8: control, not decoration
model_answers.transcript:
What I'd like to be better at is swimming, which at thirty-one is not an easy thing to say out loud.

I can swim in the narrow sense that I do not sink. Swimming properly is another matter entirely. Two hundred metres in and I'm draped over the end of the lane getting my breath back, and the reason is simply that nobody has ever corrected a single thing I do. I taught myself in a lake at about eight, by watching my brother and copying him inaccurately, and that is still, twenty-three years later, the stroke I am using. Nobody has had cause to tell me otherwise, because nobody has ever watched.

What improvement would take is depressingly clear. There are technique sessions at the pool twice a week, and the only real obstacle is that I would have to attend them instead of telling myself I'll work it out alone. Then there's the breathing. I take air on one side only, which pulls me off line, and habits of that age do not go quietly. Twenty-three years is a long time to be leaning to the left.

As to why any of this matters — I ran every morning for years until I did something irreversible to a knee, and swimming is the one thing left that empties my head the same way. Were I to reach a kilometre unbroken, I suspect what I'd actually have recovered is the hour, rather than the distance.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion with 'were I to' where band 7 used a standard second conditional.
'Draped over', 'pulls me off line', 'do not go quietly' — vivid but unshowy.
The close distinguishes what he wants from what he says he wants.

annotations.span: Were I to reach a kilometre unbroken
annotations.label: Inversion for the conditional
annotations.why: Same meaning as 'if I reached', one register higher, still speakable.

annotations.span: habits of that age do not go quietly
annotations.label: Personification with a negative
annotations.why: A short abstract subject plus a human verb reads as confident speech.

annotations.span: draped over the end of the lane
annotations.label: One verb replaces a clause
annotations.why: 'Draped' carries exhaustion and posture together in a single word.

annotations.span: I did something irreversible to a knee
annotations.label: Precision through vagueness
annotations.why: Naming the effect rather than the injury sounds like real speech.

annotations.span: what I'd actually have recovered is the hour, rather than the distance
annotations.label: Reframes the goal at the close
annotations.why: Ending by correcting your own stated aim is the strongest finish available.

model_answers.transcript:
The hobby I'd talk about is fixing up old bicycles, which I've been doing for about eleven years now.

It started more or less by accident. A neighbour moved out and left a bicycle in our shed — a heavy old thing with a bent wheel and no brakes to speak of — and rather than take it to the tip I decided I'd have a look at it. I knew nothing whatsoever about bicycles at that point. It took me two months, a great many internet videos and one very patient man in a bike shop, but eventually the thing worked. The back wheel alone took three separate attempts. I'm not sure I've been that pleased with myself since.

These days it's a Sunday morning job. A couple of hours most weeks, more if something's genuinely stuck. I pick bikes up cheaply, do them up over a month or two, and then give them away — I've handed on four so far, which is a good deal more satisfying than selling them would be. None of them costs more than about thirty pounds to start with.

The reason it's survived when other things haven't is that it's the exact opposite of my job. At work nothing is ever really finished and half the problems belong to somebody else. Whereas a bent wheel is a bent wheel. It's in front of you, it's yours, and when it's straight you can see that it's straight. That sounds like a small thing, and eleven years suggests otherwise.

The one that's lasted is fixing up old bicycles, which I've been at for something like eleven years.

It began by accident, as most of these things do. A neighbour moved out and abandoned a bicycle in our shed — heavy, bent wheel, brakes in name only — and instead of taking it to the tip I thought I'd see what could be done with it. I knew absolutely nothing. Two months, an unreasonable number of videos and one extremely patient man in a bike shop later, the thing rode. The back wheel alone took three goes. I don't think I've been quite so pleased with myself before or since.

It's a Sunday morning habit now. Two hours most weeks, longer when something refuses to move. I buy them cheaply, work on them across a month or so, and then hand them on — four have gone to friends, which beats selling them by a distance I can't really explain. Nothing I buy costs more than about thirty pounds.

What's kept it going, when so much else has fallen by the wayside, is that it is the precise inverse of my working life. At work, nothing concludes and half of every problem belongs to somebody down the corridor. A bent wheel, on the other hand, is a bent wheel. It sits in front of you, it belongs to nobody else, and when you have straightened it, it is visibly straight and it is done.

model_answers.label: Where the plateau sits
model_answers.transcript:
I want to describe one tradition of my country that I did it. It is a bread day in the village of my aunt, before the spring holiday.

The village is small, maybe four hours from my city. All the families bring the dough to one big oven and they cook the bread together. This oven is very old, I think more than one hundred years.

I go there when I was twenty-two. Before that I always say no, because it is early and it is boring for me. But my mother asked me many times, so I went.

We arrive at six in the morning and there is already a queue. I had to make the dough with my hands for one hour, and my arms were killing me. Then you must make the shape, and my shape was very bad, everybody was laughing.

In that moment I felt embarrassed and I want to go home. But now when I think about it, I feel different. It was nice to do something that my grandmother also did. So this is the tradition that I took part in it.

what_caps_it.point: 'That I did it' twice, and the past narrative keeps slipping into the present.
Five paragraphs of equal weight; the feeling gets fifteen seconds at the very end.
'Very old', 'very bad', 'boring', 'nice' — the evaluation runs on four flat words.

annotations.label: One idiom that lands
annotations.why: Keep this — a physical detail does more than any adjective could.

annotations.why: 'A tradition that I took part in' — the relative already carries the object.

annotations.span: I go there when I was twenty-two. Before that I always say no
annotations.label: Present verbs inside a past story
annotations.why: 'I went... I'd always said no' — anchor the tense and hold it.

annotations.span: We arrive at six in the morning and there is already a queue.
annotations.label: Background needs past continuous
annotations.why: 'We arrived at six and a queue was already forming' fixes both verbs.

annotations.span: So this is the tradition that I took part in it.

model_answers.label: The same morning at band 7
model_answers.transcript:
The occasion I'd describe is a bread-baking morning that happens in my aunt's village every spring, the day before the main holiday. Every family brings their dough down to one communal oven and the whole thing gets baked together.

The village is tiny — four hours from where I grew up, three streets and an oven that's supposedly two hundred years old. I'd been going there as a child and doing absolutely nothing, and I finally took part properly when I was twenty-two. Until then I'd always found a reason not to. It starts at five in the morning, which was most of the reason.

By the time we got there at six the queue was already halfway down the lane. My job turned out to be kneading for the best part of an hour, which sounds straightforward and is not. After that you shape the loaves, and mine came out looking like something a child had made. The woman next to me rearranged two of them without saying anything at all, which was somehow worse than a comment. The oven itself was too hot to stand anywhere near for long.

At the time I was mortified, and I spent the walk back working out how soon I could reasonably leave. Looking back, though, I'm oddly glad about the whole thing. Not because of the bread, which was ordinary. It was more that my grandmother had stood in that queue, and until that morning that had been a story rather than something I'd done.

what_lifts_it.point: Past perfect twice for backshift, and past continuous holding the background.
'Found a reason not to', 'mortified', 'somehow worse than a comment' — precise.
The feeling is split into then and now, which is what the fourth bullet asks for.

annotations.span: three streets and an oven that's supposedly two hundred years old
annotations.label: Builds the place in one line
annotations.why: Two concrete nouns and a number put the listener in the village.

annotations.span: I'd been going there as a child and doing absolutely nothing
annotations.label: Perfect continuous for the years before
annotations.why: It shows a long habit that ended, without a single date.

annotations.span: Until then I'd always found a reason not to.
annotations.label: Past perfect for what came before
annotations.why: One backshifted sentence explains years of avoidance in eight words.

annotations.span: which sounds straightforward and is not
annotations.label: Understatement, five words
annotations.why: Correcting the listener's assumption is a cheap way to sound natural.

annotations.span: The woman next to me rearranged two of them without saying anything at all
annotations.label: Shows the judgement, doesn't state it
annotations.why: Report the action and let the examiner feel the embarrassment.

annotations.span: At the time I was mortified
annotations.label: One word instead of three
annotations.why: 'Mortified' says badly embarrassed and is worth having ready.

annotations.span: Looking back, though, I'm oddly glad about the whole thing.
annotations.label: Turns to the present judgement
annotations.why: 'Looking back' is the signal that the last bullet has started.

annotations.span: that had been a story rather than something I'd done
annotations.label: Stress falls on 'done'
annotations.why: Let the pitch drop hard on the final word so the turn closes cleanly.

model_answers.label: The top of the range
model_answers.transcript:
What I'd describe is a bread morning in my aunt's village, held the day before the main spring holiday, when every household carries its dough down to one shared oven and the lot goes in together.

The village amounts to three streets and that oven, which is said to be two hundred years old and probably isn't. I'd been taken there every year as a child and had contributed nothing whatsoever. Not until I was twenty-two did I actually take part, largely because the thing begins at five in the morning and I had spent a decade finding that unanswerable.

We arrived at six to find the queue already halfway down the lane. My allotted job was kneading, for something close to an hour, which sounds undemanding and is the opposite of it. The dough had been sitting under a cloth in the back of the car since four. Then came the shaping, at which I was conspicuously poor. The woman beside me quietly reshaped two of my loaves and said nothing, which stung considerably more than criticism would have. None of it had been explained to me; you were simply expected to watch.

I was mortified at the time and spent the walk back calculating how early I could decently leave. What I feel now is harder to name. The bread itself was unremarkable. But my grandmother had queued in that lane, and up to that morning that had been a piece of family furniture rather than anything I had physically done.

what_lifts_it.point: Negative inversion after 'not until', against band 7's plain statement order.
'Conspicuously poor', 'stung', 'family furniture' — chosen for shade, not size.
The close admits the feeling is hard to name instead of tidying it away.

annotations.span: Not until I was twenty-two did I actually take part
annotations.label: Negative inversion
annotations.why: Front 'not until' and invert the subject and auxiliary — one sentence lifts the register.

annotations.span: which is said to be two hundred years old and probably isn't
annotations.label: Reported passive, then a flat denial
annotations.why: 'Is said to be' lets you report a claim without owning it.

annotations.span: which stung considerably more than criticism would have
annotations.label: A verb doing emotional work
annotations.why: 'Stung' carries the feeling that three adjectives would only approximate.

annotations.span: a piece of family furniture
annotations.label: Metaphor made from plain words
annotations.why: Ordinary vocabulary in an unexpected pairing outperforms any rare word.

annotations.span: What I feel now is harder to name.
annotations.label: Refuses the tidy answer
annotations.why: Admitting the feeling is complicated reads as honesty, not as hesitation.

questions: Why do young people abandon customs their grandparents took for granted?
Are traditions changing faster now than they were fifty years ago?
What would a country actually be like with no shared customs at all?

question_notes.answer_shape: Name a practical cause and a social one, then say which does more damage.

question_notes.answer_shape: Compare rate of change, then name what makes now different mechanically.
question_notes.watch_out: Avoid pure nostalgia — say what has been gained as well.

question_notes.answer_shape: Second conditional, one concrete absence, then what would fill the gap.
question_notes.watch_out: Something always fills the space. Say what, or the answer sounds unfinished.

questions: Will local customs survive when young people everywhere watch the same things?
Whose job is it to record customs before they vanish — families, schools or the state?
Is it a loss when a country's young people take up habits from elsewhere?
part3_themes.counterpoint: every culture has always borrowed, so calling it loss just means you preferred an earlier mixture
part3_themes.counter_probe: Hasn't every culture always been a borrowed mixture anyway?

question_notes.answer_shape: Predict, hedge, then name which kind of custom is most protected.
question_notes.watch_out: Distinguish customs tied to food and family from those tied to media.

question_notes.watch_out: Recording is not preserving. Say whether the distinction matters.

question_notes.answer_shape: Name the gain, name what is displaced, then commit to a verdict.
